topic: Binary Rhythms: Solving the Towers of Hanoi with Binary Counting
target_audience: High school or early university computer science and math students

outline.topic: Binary Rhythms: Solving the Towers of Hanoi with Binary Counting
outline.target_audience: High school or early university computer science and math students

sections.title: The Legend and the Logic
sections.content: Introduce the Towers of Hanoi puzzle: 3 pegs and 'n' disks of different sizes. Explain the goal (move all disks to the last peg) and the two strict rules: move only one disk at a time, and never place a larger disk on a smaller one. Present the puzzle as a sequence of moves that follows a hidden mathematical rhythm.
sections.example: Visualize a 3-disk puzzle. To move the stack, it takes exactly 7 moves ($2^3 - 1$). Imagine a small robot named 'Bit' attempting to solve it but getting confused by the recursive steps.

sections.title: Prerequisite: The Binary Heartbeat
sections.content: Introduce binary counting as a visual 'odometer'. Explain that in binary, the rightmost bit flips every step, the second bit every two steps, and the third every four steps. This section builds the foundation for mapping these 'flips' to disk movements.
sections.example: An animation showing a 3-bit counter: 001, 010, 011, 100... Highlight the 'rightmost bit that changes' in each step. For example, moving from 011 (3) to 100 (4) changes the 3rd bit from the right.

sections.title: The Magic Mapping Rule
sections.content: Connect the binary counter to the disks. The rule is simple: In move 'm', identify the rightmost bit that changed in the binary representation of 'm'. The position of that bit (1st, 2nd, or 3rd) tells you exactly which disk to move (Disk 1, Disk 2, or Disk 3).
sections.example: On Move 1 (001), the 1st bit changes -> Move Disk 1. On Move 2 (010), the 2nd bit is the rightmost change -> Move Disk 2. On Move 3 (011), the 1st bit changes again -> Move Disk 1.

sections.title: Directional Parity: Where does the disk go?
sections.content: Introduce the 'Cyclic Rule' for placement. For a set of disks, Disk 1 always moves in one direction (A -> B -> C -> A) if the total number of disks is odd, and the other way if even. This eliminates the 'which peg?' guesswork.
sections.example: Visualizing Disk 1 as a fast-moving 'scout' jumping pegs in a clockwise circle, while larger disks follow a slower, counter-clockwise rhythm. If Disk 1 is on Peg A and needs to move, it *must* go to Peg B based on the parity rule.

sections.title: Visualizing the Fractal Path
sections.content: Summarize the relationship between binary counting and the Sierpinski Triangle. Show that the state space of the Towers of Hanoi actually forms a fractal. When you follow the binary counting method, you are tracing a Hamiltonian path along the edges of a Sierpinski Gasket.
sections.example: The camera zooms out from the 3-disk puzzle to show a 6-disk puzzle. As the binary counter counts rapidly, the movements trace a perfect triangular fractal shape on the screen, showing the beauty of mathematical efficiency.

storyboard.title: The Legend and the Logic
lecture_lines: Meet the Towers of Hanoi puzzle: three pegs, 'n' disks.
Move all disks to the final peg following two rules.
One disk at a time; never place larger on smaller.
animations: Fade in three vertical pegs labeled A, B, and C in #FFFFFF.
Stack three disks (Small, Med, Large) in #FF5733, #33FF57, #3357FF on Peg A.
Move the Smallest disk (#FF5733) from Peg A to Peg C.
Move the Medium disk (#33FF57) from Peg A to Peg B.
Overlay a large red #FF0000 cross when the Large disk attempts to cover the Medium one.

storyboard.title: Prerequisite: The Binary Heartbeat
lecture_lines: Binary counting acts like a rhythmic visual odometer.
Each move flips specific bits in a repeating cycle.
The rightmost bit changes every single step.
animations: Display the binary sequence '0 0 0' in #FFFFFF at screen center.
Increment to '0 0 1' and flash the rightmost digit in #FFFF00.
Increment to '0 1 0' and flash the middle digit in #FFFF00.

storyboard.title: The Magic Mapping Rule
lecture_lines: Every binary change dictates which disk to move.
Identify the rightmost bit that changed in the move.
Bit position determines the disk number to move.
animations: Show binary '0 0 1' (1st bit changed) and highlight Disk 1 in #FF5733.
Show binary '0 1 0' (2nd bit changed) and highlight Disk 2 in #33FF57.
Show binary '0 1 1' (1st bit changed) and highlight Disk 1 in #FF5733.
Show binary '1 0 0' (3rd bit changed) and highlight Disk 3 in #3357FF.
Create a visual link (glowing line) between the flipped bit position and the disk index.

storyboard.title: Directional Parity: Where does the disk go?
lecture_lines: Where should the disk go? Follow the parity rule.
For odd disks, move disk 1 in clockwise steps.
For even disks, move disk 1 in counter-clockwise steps.
animations: Arrange three peg icons in a circular layout with arrows indicating clockwise direction.
Move a Small disk icon clockwise between peg icons to show the #00FFFF path.
Highlight the 'Even' or 'Odd' total disk count text in #FFFF00 to show the rule trigger.

storyboard.title: Visualizing the Fractal Path
lecture_lines: Disk movements trace a beautiful, hidden fractal path.
The state space forms a perfect Sierpinski Triangle.
Binary counting maps a perfect Hamiltonian path through it.
animations: Draw a simple triangle connecting three points labeled as puzzle states.
Subdivide the triangle into four smaller ones to begin the fractal.
Trace a path through the vertices as the binary counter increments rapidly.
Zoom out to display a multi-level Sierpinski Gasket in #00FFFF.
Fade the fractal into a sequence of moves being solved on pegs.
